title: Mastery Challenge: US History
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of US History Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: first peoples, colonies, revolution, the republic, a house divided, war and Reconstruction, industry, world power, civil rights and how historians argue.

cards.headline: The US History Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from the first Americans to how historians argue. Level 1 asked how an old land became a young nation; now see how much of that story you can tell. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: US History: mastered
learned: How Native nations, enslaved people, women and immigrants shaped the American story, not only its presidents.
How thirteen colonies became a republic, and why its compromises over slavery could not hold.
Why slavery drove secession and the Civil War, and how Reconstruction’s promise was won and lost.
How industry, two world wars and the Cold War made the US a world power, and what the civil rights movement won at home.
How to weigh historians’ rival explanations against the evidence from the time.

questions.prompt: Why did epidemics hit Native nations so hard after 1492?

options.label: No one there had met Eurasia’s crowd diseases before
Native nations had no healers or medicines of their own
options.rationale: Native nations had their own healers; the problem was germs no one had met.

options.label: Europeans spread disease on purpose everywhere they went
options.rationale: Epidemics spread largely without anyone planning them.

options.label: The climate of the Americas made every disease worse
options.rationale: The cause was new germs, not the climate.

questions.explanation: Before 1492 the Americas had none of the acute infectious diseases, such as smallpox and measles, so populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650.

questions.prompt: The SlaveVoyages database estimates how many Africans were forced aboard ships to the Americas?

options.label: About 388,000
options.rationale: That is about how many were landed in mainland North America.

options.label: About 1.8 million
options.rationale: That is roughly how many died on the way.

options.label: About 10.7 million
options.rationale: That is about how many survived the crossing.

options.label: About 12.5 million

questions.explanation: SlaveVoyages estimates about 12.5 million were forced aboard and about 10.7 million survived.

questions.prompt: What persuaded France to openly ally with the United States in 1778?

options.label: The Boston Tea Party
options.rationale: That was a protest in 1773.

options.label: News of the American victory at Saratoga
The Declaration of Sentiments
options.rationale: That was written at Seneca Falls in 1848.

options.label: The Treaty of Paris
options.rationale: That treaty ended the war in 1783.

questions.explanation: News of Saratoga persuaded France’s foreign minister to choose an open alliance, signed on February 6, 1778.

questions.prompt: Why does the election of 1800 matter so much in American history?

options.label: Power passed peacefully between rival parties for the first time
It was the first election in which women could vote
options.rationale: Women won the national vote in 1920.

options.label: It made George Washington the first president
options.rationale: Washington was elected in 1789.

options.label: It replaced the Articles of Confederation with the Constitution
options.rationale: The Constitution replaced the Articles earlier.

questions.explanation: In 1800 power passed peacefully from Adams’s Federalists to Jefferson’s Republicans for the first time.

questions.prompt: The Supreme Court ruled for the Cherokee in Worcester v. Georgia (1832). What happened next?

options.label: Georgia returned the Cherokee land it had seized
options.rationale: Georgia ignored the ruling.

options.label: Congress repealed the Indian Removal Act in response
options.rationale: The Removal Act stayed in force.

options.label: Georgia ignored it, and Jackson declined to enforce it
The Cherokee moved west on their own that same year
options.rationale: Forced removal came in 1838.

questions.explanation: Georgia ignored the ruling and Jackson declined to enforce it: a court can decide, but someone else has to act.

questions.prompt: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect in 1863. In which places did it leave slavery untouched?

options.label: In Confederate areas still fighting the Union
options.rationale: Those were exactly the areas it declared free.

options.label: In loyal border states and Union-held Confederate areas
Only in Washington, DC, where Congress ruled directly
options.rationale: The DC slave trade had ended in 1850; the Proclamation didn’t single out DC.

options.label: Nowhere: it ended slavery in every state at once
options.rationale: The 13th Amendment ended slavery everywhere later.

questions.explanation: It applied only to areas in rebellion, leaving slavery untouched in the loyal border states and Union-held Confederate areas.

questions.prompt: How did the Dawes Act of 1887 cost Native nations most of their land without a battle?

options.label: It moved every Native nation to Indian Territory in Oklahoma
options.rationale: That was not what the Dawes Act did.

options.label: It banned Native families from farming reservation land
options.rationale: It pushed Native families to farm allotments.

options.label: It handed reservation land to the railroads as grants
options.rationale: It sold leftover land to non-Native settlers.

options.label: It broke reservations into family plots and sold the rest

questions.explanation: Reservations were split into 160-acre allotments, the leftover land sold; holdings fell from about 138 million acres to about 48 million by 1934.

questions.prompt: Americans argued in 1899 over annexing the Philippines. Which argument came from the Anti-Imperialist League rather than annexation’s backers?

options.label: Holding the islands would open valuable trade with Asia
options.rationale: That was a backers’ argument: they wanted Asian trade.

options.label: Filipinos were not yet ready to govern themselves
options.rationale: Backers made that claim; the Filipinos’ own war for independence answered it.

options.label: Ruling Filipinos without consent betrayed the Declaration
If the US left, Germany or Japan would take the islands
options.rationale: That fear was the backers’ argument.

questions.explanation: Carnegie, Twain, Gompers and the League quoted the Declaration: governments derive “their just powers from the consent of the governed.” Backers pointed to trade, doubts about self-rule and rival empires.

questions.prompt: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) allowed segregation if facilities were “equal.” Why did NAACP lawyers first challenge it in graduate and law schools?

options.label: The Court had already overturned Plessy for colleges
options.rationale: Plessy stood until Brown in 1954.

options.label: Graduate schools were federal, so states had no say
options.rationale: They were state schools, like the Texas law school in Sweatt v. Painter.

options.label: Southern states had already agreed to integrate them
options.rationale: States fought these cases in court.

options.label: States rarely had any separate Black school there at all

questions.explanation: Where no separate Black school existed, “separate but equal” was plainly false. Thurgood Marshall’s lawyers won there first, case by case, before Brown.

questions.prompt: Two answers to why the Deep South seceded: the declarations of causes of 1860 and 1861, and the later Lost Cause. Why do historians trust the declarations?

options.label: They were written by neutral observers from Europe
options.rationale: The seceding states wrote them themselves.

options.label: They were written by the decision-makers, at the time
They say secession was mostly about tariffs and taxes
options.rationale: Several named the defense of slavery.

options.label: They were published after the war, with hindsight
options.rationale: That describes the Lost Cause writings, which historians largely consider false.

questions.explanation: The declarations are primary evidence from the people who decided, and several named the defense of slavery. The Lost Cause came after defeat and contradicts them.
